title: Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses
description: Omar Marques | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesRobinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-exp
body: Omar Marques | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesRobinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30,  compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 51 cents vs. 56 cents expectedRevenue: $1.42 billion vs. $1.42 billion expectedRobinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity. Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million. Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

schema.headline: Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

title: UBS pretax profits jump 27% in third quarter to $3.59 billion as wealth inflows surge
description: This photograph shows a sign of Swiss giant banking UBS at a branch in Zurich on March 4, 2026. Fabrice Coffrini | AFP | Getty ImagesUBS reported a pr
body: This photograph shows a sign of Swiss giant banking UBS at a branch in Zurich on March 4, 2026. Fabrice Coffrini | AFP | Getty ImagesUBS reported a pretax profit of almost $3.6 billion in the third quarter, up 27% year over year, largely in line with consensus forecasts.The Swiss banking and asset management giant saw strong net inflows into its global wealth management business.Net profit was $2.7 billion for the third quarter, in line with estimates.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconUBS shares are up by around a quarter this yearThe Zurich-headquartered lender's common equity tier (CET) 1 capital ratio — a measure of a bank's solvency — reached 14.7% during the period, up from 14.4% the previous quarter.Strong inflows into its global wealth management business supported performance, with net new assets reaching $55.1 billion by the end of the quarter. UBS recorded $12.5 billion in client commitments across its wealth management and asset management businesses.In its third-quarter earnings statement Wednesday, the bank said the integration of Credit Suisse is "firmly on track" to be completed by year-end, delivering a total of $13.7 billion in cumulative cost savings, above earlier expectations of $13.5 billion.UBS battles with Swiss government over risk toolsUBS remains locked in an ongoing wrangle with the Swiss government over proposals for increased capital buffers, aimed at insulating taxpayers from any future banking crisis and contagion from the bank's foreign subsidiaries following the Credit Suisse debacle.The bank is seen as systemically important to the Swiss economy. The country's upper house of parliament voted last month to require UBS to hold 90% of Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital, or about $16 billion in extra shares, as collateral to support its foreign subsidiaries. The level currently stands at around 45%. UBS wants it to be no more than 50%.Speaking with CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" Wednesday, Ermotti said the bank's clients expect it to be competitive. "90% would not, long-term, allow us to be a competitive player," Ermotti told CNBC's Carolin Roth. "I'm very concerned about this development."In an earlier statement, Ermotti said UBS' strong third-quarter performance underlines the benefits of its diversified global business model, adding that the lender remains "strategically committed to its diversified business model and its global and regional footprint."

schema.headline: UBS pretax profits jump 27% in third quarter to $3.59 billion as wealth inflows surge

title: Luxury round-the-world cruise ends abruptly as fuel costs skyrocket
description: Villa Vie Residences' Odyssey cruise ship passengers sit on an EV vehicle at a hotel in Sihanoukville, Preah Sihanouk province, on October 28, 2026. A
body: Villa Vie Residences' Odyssey cruise ship passengers sit on an EV vehicle at a hotel in Sihanoukville, Preah Sihanouk province, on October 28, 2026. Around 200 passengers who paid to live on a cruise ship while travelling the world were abruptly left in a Cambodian port after the company ran out of money, an official said on October 28. (Photo by TANG CHHIN Sothy / AFP via Getty Images)Tang Chhin Sothy | Afp | Getty ImagesA luxury cruise around the world has abruptly stopped, stranding passengers in Cambodia, as its operator blamed skyrocketing fuel costs.The Villa Vie Odyssey, a luxury vessel with rooms costing up to $11,000 a month, will disembark passengers and crew and find temporary accommodation, per a Tuesday online release.The vessel can carry up to 650 passengers, according to its U.S.-based operator Villa Vie Residences, and has been on a continuous voyage around the world for two years since it departed Belfast, Northern Ireland.Its amenities include a fitness center and spa, a business center, three restaurants, five bars and lounges and complimentary alcoholic beverages.The cruise drew international attention as it was marketed as a residential cruise offering a permanent home at sea while visiting hundreds of destinations.An aerial view shows the Villa Vie Residences' cruise ship Odyssey docked at Sihanoukville port in Preah Sihanouk province on October 28, 2026. Around 200 passengers who paid to live on a cruise ship while travelling the world were abruptly left in a Cambodian port after the company ran out of money, an official said on October 28. (Photo by Suy Se / AFP via Getty Images)Suy Se | Afp | Getty ImagesThe ship was due to arrive at Phu Quoc, a Vietnamese island, later this week, and from there travel to destinations including India, South Africa, Brazil and Australia, before docking in Gibraltar in August 2030."Extraordinary increases" in fuel costs meant the company would need to restructure and recapitalize its business over the next 60 days, Villa Vie Residences said in an online statement. "No outcome is assured," it added.The company said monthly fuel costs per cabin had risen from $1,800 to as much as $8,000 in parts of Asia, which represents a 344% rise, according to CNBC's calculations."The company cannot simply pass increases of that scale on to residents, and the resulting shortfall has placed its current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure," the statement said.It added that, since the Iran war began on Feb. 28, "we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port.""Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs," the company added.- CNBC's Celia Fernandez contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Luxury round-the-world cruise ends abruptly as fuel costs skyrocket

title: At least 68 people dead in high-speed Spain train crash
description: Emergency teams work at the scene of a collision involving two high-speed trains near Urda station in Toledo province, Spain, on October 28, 2026. Bur
body: Emergency teams work at the scene of a collision involving two high-speed trains near Urda station in Toledo province, Spain, on October 28, 2026. Burak Akbulut | Anadolu | Getty ImagesAt least 68 people have been killed in a collision between two trains in the Spanish province of Toledo, authorities have said.The high-speed trains collided shortly before 9:15 a.m. local time (4:15 a.m. ET), when emergency services were deployed to the scene. It occurred on the Madrid to Seville line.Transport Minister Óscar Puente told reporters in Madrid that the control system at the nearby town of Urda failed and six trains were stopped. One was allowed to restart and travelled 25km before hitting a stopped train at high speed, he added, saying it was "inexplicable" how this had happened.As well as those killed, 50 people were also injured, the minister said.Railway infrastructure manager Adif is investigating the sequence of events surrounding the accident, Spanish news agency EFE reported.Passengers at Santa Justa station following the train accident in Urda (Toledo), which has forced the suspension of services on the Madrid–Andalusia high-speed line Oct. 28, 2026, Seville (Andalusia, Spain).Francisco J. Olmo | Europa Press | Getty ImagesThe local Castilla-La Mancha government confirmed at least 68 people had died, higher than another high-speed crash in southern Spain that killed 45 people in January.Emiliano García-Page, the president of the region, said 24 people had died on a train operated by rail company Renfe, with the rest killed on a train operated by Iryo.More than 500 passengers were on board the two trains, newspaper El País said.Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by the Renfe train, saying the cause was "still unknown".Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said in a post on X that he was "shocked" by the accident. "If there has been any negligence, it will come to light," he later said at a press conference."If there have been failures in the safety system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness. It is clear that we have experienced two terrible tragedies involving high-speed rail within the same year."Emergency services work at the site of a train crash between a high speed Renfe AVE train and Iryo train around 150kms south of Madrid between Urda and Los Yebenes in the province of Toledo, on October 28, 2026. Javier Soriano | Afp | Getty ImagesSanchez's political future will be tested in a snap election on Nov. 29, which he called following widespread unrest over Spain's housing crisis. Santiago Abascal, leader of the far-right Vox party — which is expected to make gains when Spain goes to the polls — pointed the finger at Sanchez's government over the train accident on Wednesday. "Tragedy again. Rage again over the neglect, the ruin, and the betrayal suffered by the Spanish people," he said in a post on X.— CNBC's Charlotte Reed contributed to this article.

schema.headline: At least 68 people dead in high-speed Spain train crash

title: Ford Motor is set to report earnings after the bell. Here's what Wall Street expects
description: A close-up view shows a standalone Ford corporate Blue Oval logo monument sign at a vehicle dealership in Santaquin, Utah, United States, on August 30
body: A close-up view shows a standalone Ford corporate Blue Oval logo monument sign at a vehicle dealership in Santaquin, Utah, United States, on August 30, 2026. Charles-McClintock Wilson | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesDETROIT — Ford Motor is set to announce third-quarter earnings after the markets close Wednesday.Here's what Wall Street expects, based on average analysts' estimates compiled by LSEG:Earnings per share: 40 cents adjusted, estimatedAutomotive revenue: $46.24 billion estimatedThose results would mark a 2% decline in revenue compared with a year earlier and a roughly 11% decrease in adjusted earnings per share. Ford's 2025 third-quarter results included $47.19 billion in automotive revenue, net income of $2.4 billion and earnings per share of 45 cents adjusted.A main focus for investors will be Ford's F-Series pickup trucks, including its crucial F-150. The automaker has been recovering from supplier issues that affected truck production for much of the past year, but experienced a disruption in F-150 manufacturing due to a separate, unrelated supplier problem toward the end of September.Ford reported production of the F-150 declined from more than 57,500 units in August to less than 43,000 in September. The automaker said the disruption is "containable within" its existing 2026 adjusted earnings guidance.Wall Street analysts generally expect Ford to maintain its 2026 outlook, but they differ on how the F-150 production disruption will ultimately affect the automaker's third-quarter results. They're also watching for any changes or surprises in the company's warranty costs.Ford's 2026 guidance includes adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $10 billion and $11 billion and adjusted free cash flow of $6 billion to $7 billion.

schema.headline: Ford Motor is set to report earnings after the bell. Here's what Wall Street expects

title: Wendy's shares jump 15% as Nelson Peltz's Trian offers $1.4 billion to buy burger chain
description: Signage for a Wendy's restaurant in Brampton, Ontario, on April 21, 2026. Mike Campbell | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesA group of investors led by Nelson Pe
body: Signage for a Wendy's restaurant in Brampton, Ontario, on April 21, 2026. Mike Campbell | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesA group of investors led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Fund Management has offered $1.4 billion to buy Wendy's, according to a regulatory filing Wednesday.The group has offered $7.35 per share in cash to take the burger chain private, paying a 20% premium to Tuesday's closing price. In addition to Trian, it includes investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners, plus Flynn Group, one of Wendy's largest franchisees.Wendy's shares spiked about 15% in morning trading following the offer. The Wall Street Journal first reported Peltz's proposal.Wendy's did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. Trian declined to comment beyond the filing.The take-private deal offer comes after a tough two-year stretch for the burger chain. Wendy's stock has tumbled 65% over that period, including Wednesday's gains. For six straight quarters, the company has reported same-store sales declines. Wendy's is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings before the bell on Nov. 5.Wendy's challenges have made the company a cheaper acquisition target for Peltz, whose history with the brand dates back to an activist campaign he led more than two decades ago. Budget-conscious diners have been eating out less often, and Wendy's and its rivals have leaned into discounts to lure consumers into restaurants. Wendy's has also dealt with a revolving door of chief executives, who have had different ideas about turnaround strategies for the struggling chain."In our view, a take private makes sense as Wendy's turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the challenged state of the lower income consumer and soft state of the quick service burger category," TD Cowen analyst Andrew Charles wrote in a note to clients on Wednesday.In May, former Potbelly CEO Bob Wright joined Wendy's as its latest chief executive, after his former employer went private. In his first earnings conference call with analysts in August, he was candid about what he views as the chain's biggest issues, like muddled value offerings, inconsistent execution at its restaurants and too many one-off promotions.Trian previously explored a takeover of Wendy's in 2022, but later decided against it. The firm and affiliated parties own a 16.25% stake in Wendy's, according to the regulatory filing, making them the company's largest shareholder.

schema.headline: Wendy's shares jump 15% as Nelson Peltz's Trian offers $1.4 billion to buy burger chain

title: FEC campaign finance system offline days before midterms after hackers reportedly target site
description: People take part in early voting in the Midterm Elections at a polling center at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Manhattan, New York City, on October
body: People take part in early voting in the Midterm Elections at a polling center at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Manhattan, New York City, on October 24, 2026. Selcuk Acar | Anadolu | Getty ImagesThe Federal Election Commission said Tuesday night that it identified the issue affecting its electronic filing system and was implementing a fix, after reports that a hacker or hackers had targeted the agency's systems days before the midterm elections.But the system remained offline early Wednesday, cutting off a key window into campaign money just as late-election spending surges.An FEC electronic filings official told campaign compliance firms Monday night that a "bad actor" was attempting to breach the agency's systems and that public-facing services had been shut down, according to an email obtained by Reuters. The filing system has been offline since around 10 p.m. ET on Monday.The FEC has not said who was behind the reported breach attempt, whether anyone gained access to its systems or whether any data was compromised. Previously filed reports remain searchable. The FEC told CNBC that the agency's IT staff is working to restore the service.In the final 20 days before an election, candidate committees must report certain contributions or loans of $1,000 or more within 48 hours, while political committees and outside groups must disclose certain spending within 24 hours.Those rules are designed to give voters a near-real-time view of the money flooding into races when it matters most.For example, Elon Musk's America PAC reported nearly $6.8 million in independent expenditures for communications disseminated Oct. 20, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. Spending on that scale normally becomes public almost immediately, but with the filing system down, new money can pour into races while the public stays in the dark.The potential blind spot comes as the 2026 midterms become the most expensive U.S. election cycle on record by political advertising, with $11.21 billion spent or reserved as of Monday night, according to AdImpact.Political committees and other outside groups reported nearly $610 million in independent expenditures for communications disseminated from Oct. 20 through Oct. 26 — an average of about $87 million a day — according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings.The outage also hits an already weakened agency. The six-member FEC, an independent agency that oversees campaign finance laws and has no role in administering elections, has had just two members since October 2025 and has lacked the four commissioners it needs to take official action since May 2025. Career staff have continued processing disclosures and running day-to-day operations.The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency did not respond to a request for comment. The FBI deferred to the FEC.

schema.headline: FEC campaign finance system offline days before midterms after hackers reportedly target site

title: Mortgage rates fell for the second straight week, but more borrowers still sought savings in riskier loans
description: In an aerial view, two-story single family homes line the streets of a neighborhood on Sept. 23, 2026 in Thousand Oaks, California. Kevin Carter | Get
body: In an aerial view, two-story single family homes line the streets of a neighborhood on Sept. 23, 2026 in Thousand Oaks, California. Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesMortgage rates fell for the second straight week, and that finally brought consumers back to their brokers. A growing share, however, applied for riskier loans at even lower rates.Total mortgage application volume rose 3.4% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, decreased to 7.37% from 7.41%, with points increasing to 0.76 from 0.75, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. "The decline in rates gave borrowers some relief, with applications rebounding slightly, particularly conventional applications," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the MBA, in a release. "Mortgage rates are still more than a percentage point higher than the same week last year and most homeowners still have rates much lower than prevailing market rates."And that is why refinance is still running well behind where it was last year. Applications to refinance a home loan climbed 3% for the week but were 61% lower than the same week one year ago. About half of all borrowers today have a mortgage rate below 4%, according to data from the Federal Housing Finance Agency's National Mortgage Database.Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home rose 4% for the week but were still 18% lower than the same week one year ago. While mortgage rates have pulled back some in the last few weeks, they are still much higher than they were just a few months ago, and home prices are still rising. Potential homebuyers are also worried about the broader economy, and, anecdotally, some agents say buyers are waiting to see the results of the midterm elections.Get Property Play directly to your inboxCNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.Subscribe here to get access today.As borrowers search for savings, more are opting for adjustable-rate mortgages. The ARM share of applications increased to 11.3% last week, the highest level in more than a year. The average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs decreased to 6.41% from 6.46%. ARMs are considered riskier because they adjust to whatever the current market rate is at the end of their fixed term.Mortgage rates haven't moved at all to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. That is because there has not been much economic data for the bond market to react to. While the Federal Reserve is not expected to announce any change in its interest rate at Wednesday's meeting, markets could move on any commentary from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh.

schema.headline: Mortgage rates fell for the second straight week, but more borrowers still sought savings in riskier loans

title: Trump says Iran war will end 'when I want it to' as costs reportedly balloon to $47 billion
description: US President Donald Trump speaks to the media before boarding Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland on Oct. 27, 2026.Kent Nishimura | AFP | Ge
body: US President Donald Trump speaks to the media before boarding Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland on Oct. 27, 2026.Kent Nishimura | AFP | Getty ImagesU.S. President Donald Trump has reiterated his claim that the Iran war will end "whenever I want it to," but insists that Tehran cannot have a nuclear weapon.Speaking at a rally in Lubbock, Texas, Trump said "Somebody asked me before, 'When will the war in Iran end?' I said, 'Whenever I want it to end.'"Trump said it "would be very quick, but we have to have an end properly," with a "total statement" that Iran would never have a nuclear weapon.His statement comes as the president grapples with poll numbers that are near a record low due to rising energy costs and affordability issues as the U.S. heads into the midterm elections on Nov. 3.Currently, Trump's approval ratings stand at 32%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll on Monday.  Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, said on Oct. 12 that the war was costing American families an average of $2,000 so far, where $1,100 comes from higher energy costs, $540 from heightened interest rate costs and $360 due to increased military spending.The Iran conflict shows no sign of winding down, with Trump saying that he will soon decide whether to "make a deal" with Iran or "finish it off."Earlier in the month, the U.S. had evacuated diplomats from Saudi Arabia, as The New York Times reported that U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for a "short but intensive" operation for strikes  on Iran after the midterm elections. An estimate by U.S. Central Command on Oct. 16, according to a report by The Hill, also revealed that the cost of the Iran war has ballooned to $47 billion, about $3 billion more than the previous numbers. The bulk of the costs was reportedly for munitions replacements at $29 billion. Washington's conflict with Iran has caused "shortfalls" in U.S. munitions, despite Trump claiming on Sept. 3 that the U.S. had  "virtually unlimited" amounts of ammunition.The massive price tag on the war does not include the costs of damaged military bases in the Middle East, which is estimated at $184 million as of June 29, according to a lead inspector general report to Congress. This figure counts damage to U.S. diplomatic facilities in four countries — Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — from Iranian strikes.Correction: The bulk of the costs was reportedly for munitions replacements at $29 billion. An earlier version misstated the figure.

schema.headline: Trump says Iran war will end 'when I want it to' as costs reportedly balloon to $47 billion

title: Why China is desperate to ship cars outside of the country
description: To understand why China is desperate to ship cars overseas, visit a dealership in Beijing.Autumn has traditionally been the peak time to buy vehicles
body: To understand why China is desperate to ship cars overseas, visit a dealership in Beijing.Autumn has traditionally been the peak time to buy vehicles in the country, but this year many showrooms are empty or shut.Car salesman Li Ke said that other than the Covid-19 pandemic, the 2026 "golden September and silver October" season, as it's known, is the slowest he's seen in his 26 years on the job."In past years, customers would come to the showrooms nonstop," he told CNBC during an interview in his deserted showroom at a complex of dealerships on the outskirts of the Chinese capital. "We would have deals to sign every day. But nowadays we see only two to three deals a week. It's a dramatic drop."Many people in China aren't buying cars because an unstable job market and a continued slide in property prices have undercut consumer confidence. The government has also scaled back incentives such as cash-for-clunkers subsidies and tax breaks to go electric, car salespeople said.Passenger car retail sales for 2026 in China totaled 13.33 million units through September, falling 21.7% from a year ago, according to the China Passenger Car Association. For the full year 2026, China's domestic passenger car retail sales are set to drop 22% to 18.5 million vehicles, the association said — under the level recorded in the first year of the pandemic.Even electric vehicles, which were once a bright spot, are down. Gasoline car sales have been declining in China because of the country's transition to electric vehicles, but sales in China of new-energy vehicles — which includes EVs — dropped by 12.8% from January through September, according to the association."Customers are watching every penny," Li said. "When looking at all the new functions on all these new models, they are weighing what is most practical, economic and worth their money over the long term. We don't see impulse buying. Because of the bad economy, people are taking more time to replace their cars." The fierce competition has led to bruising price wars in recent years, a key reason Chinese carmakers have cast their eyes overseas and why Beijing is fearful of partners like the U.S. and Europe putting up coordinated trade barriers against its massive car exports, analysts said.Industrial profits for the first nine months of the year were up 15.5% from the same period in 2025, but September showed signs of weakness relative to the prior eight months, according to China's National Bureau of Statistics. For the auto manufacturing industry specifically, profits from January to September shrank by 22.8% compared with last year.To preserve cash, Li's dealership moved out of a pricey streetside space to one with less foot traffic but that rents at a fraction of the cost.With profit margins eroding, Li said he sees little point in offering further discounts. He said the bigger hurdle is the prevailing Chinese consumer attitude toward big-ticket purchases."Chinese buyers would rather wait," he said.

schema.headline: Why China is desperate to ship cars outside of the country

title: UK brings forward defense spending target, pledging billions to Ukraine
description: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey holds the red Budget box outside 11 Downing Street ahead of the announcement of the Autumn Budget in
body: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey holds the red Budget box outside 11 Downing Street ahead of the announcement of the Autumn Budget in the House of Commons in London, United Kingdom on October 28, 2026. Wiktor Szymanowicz | Future Publishing | Getty ImagesThe U.K. has set out a target date for defense spending to rise to 3% of GDP, as the finance minister announced billions in aid for Ukraine in a "clear message to Moscow".John Healey on Wednesday set a target date of 2030 for the 3% figure, while reaffirming its NATO commitment to reach 3.5% by 2035.Healey, who resigned as defense minister under the previous government over insufficient spending, presented his first annual budget as finance minister and highlighted a "new era of threat"."Today we send a clear message to Moscow: Britain will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes," he said as he announced an additional £10 billion ($13.3 billion) in economic and military support, based on loans, export finance guarantees, as well as £500 million in urgent military funding for this winter.The government will set out the details of how it will meet its defense spending targets at the spending review next year, Healey told lawmakers."As we look ahead to the spending review, we start from a position of strength, with spending at that higher base, there will be choices we have to make about priorities," he said."Today, I'm getting work underway to get there in a fiscally sustainable way," Healey said against the backdrop of strained public finances and increasing borrowing costs.More defense news‘Project Firepower’: Inside Rheinmetall’s gunpowder expansion as Europe races to replenish its ammunitionEurope’s defense boom faces a new test: Can it actually deliver weapons?Ukraine’s drone playbook is wreaking havoc in Russia — and upending where NATO wants to investTank maker KNDS postpones IPO amid market struggles for defenseDefense stocks plummet on reports Germany is scrapping warships; Rheinmetall stock down 18%Why Europe is suddenly betting big on dronesHealey also said the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank will deploy up to £5 billion over the next four years into defence, dual-use technologies and other sectors supporting national security to strengthen the UK defense industrial base, support domestic supply chains and attract private investment.Chris Beauchamp, chief UK market analyst at investing and trading platform IG, said Healey's announcement lacked detail but "it looks like defence will get the money Healey said was needed when he was defence secretary.""The precise path will come through next year, but it seems like the spending bonanza for Rolls-Royce and others is still on the way. It just might take a little while to arrive," he added.Healey also announced that Rolls-Royce will develop its next-generation turbine engine technology in partnership with the U.K. government, in an investment worth £2.5 billion.

schema.headline: UK brings forward defense spending target, pledging billions to Ukraine

title: America's largest budget airline reports 71% jump in airfare
description: A Frontier Airlines Airbus A321 airplane goes down the runway at Los Angeles International Airport on Jan. 2, 2025, in Los Angeles, California.Kevin C
body: A Frontier Airlines Airbus A321 airplane goes down the runway at Los Angeles International Airport on Jan. 2, 2025, in Los Angeles, California.Kevin Carter | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesFrontier Airlines reported a 71% increase in airfare in the third quarter as the country's largest budget airline tried to pass along an even bigger jump in jet fuel prices. Frontier's fare revenue averaged $67.82 per passenger in the third quarter, compared with $39.74 last year. Including the budget airline's many fees, such as for checked and carry-on luggage, total revenue per passenger rose 30% on the year to $138.22.Customers kept booking despite the higher prices. Frontier's passenger count rose 18% to more than 9.8 million people in the quarter. That's a difference of 1.5 million passengers from last year. The company said demand remains strong, even at these higher prices, but Frontier still lost money. The airline widened its third-quarter loss to $104 million from a $77 million loss a year earlier. Its fuel bill soared 82% to $425 million.Frontier forecast potential adjusted profit in the fourth quarter, saying it expects to post an adjusted loss of 15 cents per share to adjusted earnings of as much as 5 cents per share.Carriers from Delta Air Lines to Frontier have said customers are mostly continuing to book flights despite higher fares, but that record jet fuel prices, their biggest cost after labor, are eroding profits.Frontier shares were up more than 9% in afternoon trading Wednesday.Frontier had eclipsed Spirit Airlines as the biggest discount carrier in the country even before that airline collapsed in May. title: The UK cuts energy bills, taxes banks and boosts defense in high-stakes budget
description: Secretary of State for Defence John Healey arrives in Downing Street to attend the weekly Cabinet meeting in London, United Kingdom on June 02, 2026.
body: Secretary of State for Defence John Healey arrives in Downing Street to attend the weekly Cabinet meeting in London, United Kingdom on June 02, 2026. Wiktor Szymanowicz | Future Publishing | Getty ImagesThe U.K.'s finance minister John Healey delivered his first fiscal budget on Wednesday, announcing funding for defense, AI initiatives and measures designed to ease cost-of-living pressures. The Autumn Budget included dozens of measures aimed largely at easing rising costs for Britain's population, but Healey was careful not to risk the ire of markets, which responded broadly positively to his plans.  Cost-of-living crisisAs a net energy importer, the U.K. is vulnerable to external energy shocks. Inflation has risen sharply this year, with surging fuel costs driving the annual inflation rate to 3.5% in September. Markets expect the Bank of England to hike interest rates next month, while government borrowing costs have risen sharply this year.The U.K. government, led by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, had promised to alleviate economic pressures ahead of the budget. On Wednesday, Healey said he would deliver "breathing space" for families, saying the country needs "radical change on energy," and citing the inflationary impact of the U.S.-Iran war — a conflict he said "we did not want."His measures included the removal of standing charges on household gas heating bills, the extension of a tax break on electricity for millions of households through July 2027, and £100 ($133) checks for those living in the four lowest local housing tax bands. This will cost £2.6 billion. Healey said tariffs would be removed on over 100 grocery products, a policy announced before the budget was officially unveiled. Small business relief from business rates — a tax on commercial premises — would be extended to include more companies in the hospitality, retail and leisure sectors. Other measures included £15 million to provide books for children, funding aimed at reducing homelessness and support for people to purchase their first home.The U.K.'s minimum wage will rise by 3.9%, while a planned cut to tax-free savings thresholds was canceled.But Healey also pledged to bring down the welfare bill, pointing to reforms to pensions and sickness benefits.But he said he would not "write off a million young people [or] see disabled people suffer the indignities of a system that has been found 'not fit for purpose.'"The U.K.'s welfare bill, which reached 10.7% of UK GDP in 2024/25, has been a contentious issue in recent years. Previous finance minister Rachel Reeves watered down her own plans to cut welfare spending after a rebellion from lawmakers within her party. AI in focusHealey also announced investments in developing — and regulating — the U.K.'s artificial intelligence industry.  "Nowhere is the necessary role for the state clearer than in artificial intelligence," he said, as he announced hundreds of millions of pounds in funding for AI security and sovereignty.He announced a "covenant" for data centers in the country, with "strict tests" they must meet: "To invest in local communities, create local jobs and protect local water supplies. In return, critical data centers will get the grid connections they need, and, where necessary, be allowed to build onsite generation while they wait," Healey said.Healey also announced tax breaks for founders, including a reduced capital gains tax rate on gains of up to £10 million.Cash would also be injected into various regional hubs, Healey said, to "unleash Britain's innovation power."Defense spending The budget also included £10 billion of additional economic and military support for Ukraine. "Today we send a clear message to Moscow: Britain will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes," he said. More funding would go to defense, he added, to ensure the country can meet its NATO spending commitments. "At the Spending Review next year, I confirm that I will set out the details of how we will meet our NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030," he said. "In this new era of threat, the demands on U.K. defense are rising."Fiscal rules maintainedHealey said his spending plans complied with the so-called fiscal rules set by his predecessor. Under those rules, the government's day-to-day spending must be funded by tax revenues rather than borrowing, and debt must be declining as a share of GDP.Alongside the budget announcements on Wednesday, the U.K.'s Office for Budget Responsibility forecast that the government would have £15 billion of fiscal headroom by the 2029/30 financial year. "Despite global challenges, this Budget puts us on track to eliminate the current budget deficit and get Britain's finances into the black within three years," Healey told lawmakers in parliament before unveiling the full details of his fiscal shake-up. The OBR forecast on Wednesday that national debt as a share of GDP would rise slightly to 83.8% next year, before steadily declining until it reaches 81.7% of GDP by the 2032 financial year. It also raised its growth forecast for the U.K., saying it now expects the economy to expand by 1.2% this year, 1% in 2027 and 1.6% in 2028.  Yields on U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, fell as Healey spoke. By 1:50 p.m. in London (9.50 a.m. ET), the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt was 2 basis points lower at 5.323%. Sterling was marginally lower against the U.S. dollar, and 0.2% lower versus the euro. Banks foot the bill Healey said Wednesday that he would raise revenue "from those who can afford to pay.""No tax rises on wages or dividends," he said. "Cutting taxes for millions of families and businesses."Banks, gambling businesses and vape shops would be taxed to help pay for the new measures, he announced.Healey — who earlier this month called Britain's banks the "jewel" in the country's economic crown — said the bank surcharge would now be raised by 3%, bringing it to 6%.Healey said the U.K.'s "world-leading banks" make a "huge contribution" to the country — and he was now asking them to fund the "breathing space" for Britain's households.The temporary measure will be implemented in January and end 15 months later.The scale of tax hikes was not as severe as some in the sector had feared, and shares in London-listed lenders moved higher on the announcement.Shares in U.K. banks rose. Barclays were last seen 3.3% higher, while Lloyds Banking Group rose more than 2.6%. NatWest Group was up 2.5%.JPMorgan Chase, whose CEO Jamie Dimon joined bankers lobbying against additional U.K. taxes last month, said in a statement that "to single out this industry for additional taxes again, one of the UK's biggest generators of growth and jobs, lacks principle.""It also overlooks that the banking industry operates in a highly competitive global marketplace," a company spokesperson said. Dimon has previously suggested it may rethink the multibillion-dollar buildout of its new headquarters in London's Canary Wharf financial district if the government is "hostile" to banks. The company said on Wednesday that it is "committed" to the U.K. — CNBC's Hugh Leask contributed to this report.

schema.headline: The UK cuts energy bills, taxes banks and boosts defense in high-stakes budget

title: Microsoft earnings will land after the close
description: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella speaks at a company event at La Defense business district in Puteaux, near Paris, on Oct. 20, 2026.Dimitar Dilkoff | AFP |
body: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella speaks at a company event at La Defense business district in Puteaux, near Paris, on Oct. 20, 2026.Dimitar Dilkoff | AFP | Getty ImagesMicrosoft is set to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday.Here's what analysts are expecting, according to LSEG:Earnings: $4.73 per share, adjustedRevenue: $90.69 billion For the fiscal first quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, Microsoft will be reporting under two operating segments for the first time since 1998. For the past 11 years it had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.Microsoft will also begin disclosing Azure cloud revenue in dollars. Analysts polled by StreetAccount are expecting $32.32 billion, which would represent growth of more than 44%. The software giant has been working to become a bigger force in artificial intelligence through infrastructure expansion and product enhancements, while continuing to produce free cash flow, unlike its fellow hyperscalers.Cloud rivals Alphabet and Amazon, which report results on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively, both showed negative free cash flow in the June quarter, while Meta said last week that it went free cash flow negative in the third quarter. As of Tuesday's close, Microsoft shares were up almost 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained about 13% over the same period.During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs, and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency.Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount projected $50.67 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases for the quarter.Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.Executives will discuss the results with analysts and issue guidance on a conference call starting at 5:30 p.m. ET.WATCH: What to expect from Microsoftwatch now

schema.headline: Microsoft earnings will land after the close

title: A Democratic win in midterms could put prediction markets and the CFTC in the hot seat
description: The Capitol in Washington, Sept. 16, 2026.Daniel Heuer | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe rise of prediction markets has confounded Washington, with lawmak
body: The Capitol in Washington, Sept. 16, 2026.Daniel Heuer | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe rise of prediction markets has confounded Washington, with lawmakers still learning how the exchanges work — and little done in Congress to support or rein in the companies. But the midterm elections may spark movement, with both platforms and their regulator set to come under increased scrutiny as part of a broader oversight agenda by the Democratic Party. For now, prediction markets have appeared as a nonpartisan issue, with both supporters and opponents on each side of the aisle. Nearly 30 prediction market-related bills have been introduced in both chambers since 2025, with most sponsored by Democrats and introduced in the House of Representatives. Those measures focus on banning or restricting congressional members and staff from participating on the platforms and prohibiting particular contracts, primarily sports-related ones.Zero have passed.With polls signaling Democrats are on track to flip the House next month, those bills and proponents seeking to tackle the industry may stand a better chance to succeed under Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries.Even beyond any sort of legislation, Democrats through committee investigative powers could confront President Donald Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr., and his advisory role with leading companies Kalshi and Polymarket, which many Democrats, and even some Republicans, fear may have been used to gain favorable regulatory rulings from the administration.The regulator in question, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, may face greater scrutiny too. Some lawmakers have worried whether the agency, after recent staffing cuts, can handle oversight of the booming prediction markets industry.The CFTC disputes that concern, telling CNBC its work in other markets proves it can handle emerging event contracts. Meanwhile, both leading platforms said they welcome engagement with lawmakers and even potential legislation as the industry grows. "We welcome scrutiny," a Polymarket spokesperson said in a statement. "We are a new concept to most and our biggest problem is typically a lack of understanding of the way our platform operates … We want to work with lawmakers and staff to ensure all the promise and value of prediction markets is captured and regulations meet the scale and scope of the massive demand for the product."Why Democrats might go after platformsWhile both parties have expressed concerns over prediction markets, where things might get more partisan is over Trump Jr.'s role as an advisor at both Kalshi and Polymarket. His venture capital firm 1789 Capital also has an investment in the latter company, though a spokesperson told CNBC that Trump Jr. doesn't sit on the firm's investment decision-making committee and "therefore has no ability to allocate capital to companies." The spokesperson added Trump Jr.'s advisory role at Polymarket was done outside of the firm's investment. Both leading prediction market companies have sought favorable CFTC rulings, including for new products and ongoing rulemaking in the emerging space, as they grow, and some lawmakers have worried how Trump Jr.'s role may impact those decisions. "I know that the appearance of conflicts of interest was significant enough that a Republican senator called for a probe into Don Trump Jr. interests and specifically his interests in polymarket and culture," said Joseph Konizeski, a former trial attorney in the CFTC, referencing a letter by Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, a skeptic of prediction markets. "So when you have a Republican senator making that sort of a public plea, I think that that tells you that it's a serious issue." The office for U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is set to be the chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee if Democrats retake the chamber, did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the president's son called the concerns on his relationship and role on the platforms as politically motivated. "Democrats are obsessed with harassing Don because of his last name, despite having zero evidence that he has actually engaged in any wrongdoing whatsoever," the spokesperson said in a statement. "Don does not ever interface with the Federal Government on behalf of any company that he advises or invests in."A person familiar with Polymarket's operations said the company's investors and advisors, such as Trump Jr., give business and strategic advice. Polymarket's internal management and legal teams handle regulatory obligations, the person added. Donald Trump Jr., co-founder of World Liberty Financial, during the Future Investment Initiative Priority Summit conference in Miami, Florida, March 27, 2026.Zak Bennett | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesBoth Kalshi and Polymarket also have relationships with Democrats too. Former President Barack Obama staffer Stephanie Cutter is a senior policy advisor at Kalshi, while Polymarket hired in September Rob Eskridge, a former chief of staff to a Democratic congressman, to lead its government relations team.Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour said last week on MS NOW that Trump Jr.'s connection to the company creates an "optics issue," but added that it has never used that relationship to gain favor with the U.S. government. Over the past nine months, Kalshi has had numerous conversations with lawmakers over Trump Jr.'s role in the company, reassuring them that the president's son solely advises on its marketing, the platform said. The company added it has seen bipartisan progress with lawmakers on how they view prediction markets by noting the benefits of a federally regulated exchange rather than one hosted offshore. Lawmakers are still learning about prediction markets, since they're so new, and that means what exact action they'll take in the area remains unclear. "They want to do some amount of investigations on this. I think they don't seem to have a broad sense of what this entails yet," a Democrat and former general counsel to a U.S. senator, who asked not to be named to speak frankly, said about policymakers. The person said sports contracts are an easier entry point for lawmakers because they can compare the contracts with sports betting.A spokesperson for Kalshi said the company welcomes legislative frameworks to tackle insider trading concerns, establish consumer protections and make clear standards on what contract types are allowed."Congress has both the opportunity and, we believe, the appetite to get this right," the spokesperson said. "Smart guardrails now will let this industry grow responsibly here at home while preventing the abuses that thrive offshore, beyond the reach of U.S. regulators."Sean Patrick Maloney, a former Democratic representative who now leads the Coalition for Prediction Markets, warned his party about moving too aggressively against the industry."Why are you going to drive that to offshore platforms that don't have the same manipulation protections that you have here?" he asked at a conference in New York City this month. He added Democrats are often too focused on opposing something just because it's "coded Trump," which he called shortsighted.CFTC in the spotlightDemocrats, and some Republicans, have expressed skepticism about the CFTC's ability to regulate these new markets, driven by concerns regarding the exchanges' sports offerings and worries about cuts the agency faced in 2025. The Government Accountability Office in July accepted a request by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., to review the commission's workforce reduction, according to a letter first reported by NPR.A win for Democrats in the U.S. Senate would likely place Warren as chair of the chamber's Banking Committee. She has been a skeptic of prediction markets, and Warren is widely expected through the committee to expand oversight of the industry's regulator, the CFTC.A representative for Warren's office declined a request for comment.CFTC spokesperson Zach Fulton rejected criticism that the agency can't handle oversight of event contracts. "The CFTC currently regulates nearly $600 trillion in notional value across U.S. derivatives markets," he said in a statement. "The Commission is more than capable of overseeing prediction markets that are less than $1 trillion notional." Fulton noted in the statement that the CFTC is on track to hire roughly 100 employees in "critical areas" by the end of 2026.Michael Selig, President Donald Trump's nominee to serve as Commodity Futures Trading Commission chairman, testifies in a Senate Agriculture Committee hearing on his nomination on Capitol Hill, Nov. 19, 2025.Jonathan Ernst | ReutersAnd the CFTC has in recent months stepped up its regulatory work in the space. For example, in July, the commission announced it was seeking public comments on proposed rulemaking regarding vertical integration within its regulated exchanges, highlighting close relationships some event contract platforms have with market makers — including platforms with affiliated or in-house market makers. Last month, the agency sent a letter to exchanges detailing concerns on "mention markets," where users place trades on what an individual will say in a speech or broadcast. The letter said those markets have a greater manipulation risk. J. Chris Giancarlo, a former CFTC chair, said the moves show the agency is building robust guardrails. "They're saying, 'this innovation should happen here, and we're duty bound to put a regulatory framework around it.'"Yet, the commission remains steadfast in its support for the novel asset class. It continues to defend platforms in disputes with states across the country who argue their sports-related offerings amount to gambling, and has continued to approve new product offerings by the exchanges. Those decisions will face greater congressional scrutiny if power in Washington changes, said David Aron, a former special counsel at the CFTC. "If the Democrats take control of either chamber, then that chamber's committees that oversee the CFTC will be a little sharper with them, call them in, demand answers," he said. "That will not be fun." Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: A Democratic win in midterms could put prediction markets and the CFTC in the hot seat
